The Data Recipient agrees to process the Data only for the following purposes agreed with the HSCIC:      
Objective for processing: 
The internet is playing an increasingly important role in healthcare.  Understanding the relationship between internet use and health outcomes is important to advance healthcare and understand the consequences of digital participation, or a lack thereof.  Both improving population health and closing digital divides are high on the agenda of UK and EU policy makers.  However, the existing literature has only partially looked at the association of internet use and health outcomes for specific conditions.  Previous studies have neither had a comprehensive review on internet use, nor did they base their insights on real-world health data.  Moreover, there is a gap in the literature as concerns the mediating mechanisms between internet use and health outcomes from a social science perspective.
The proposed research examines the research question of whether internet use is associated with health outcomes in the context of England.  More specifically, it discusses the mechanisms by which these two are associated, how the relationship varies when looking at different conceptualisations of health outcomes, and how internet use compares relative to other associative factors with health outcomes.  Finally, the research seeks to clarify whether a casual relationship between internet use and health outcomes can be determined. 
Processing activities: 
To assess the research questions outlined in the objective for processing, the University of Oxford propose a mixed methods research design with a quantitative frame and an embedded qualitative strand.  HES data is requested for the quantitative part of the research and will be analysed together with OxIS (a random sample survey on internet use in Great Britain, conducted by the Oxford Internet Institute biannually) and the UK census data.  The proposed project will use a novel methodology called “spatial microsimulation”. This methodology allows the combination of datasets based on very small geographic areas (output areas = 10‐digit OACODE) without the need to use individual‐level patient data. This represents a very privacy‐preserving way of doing research and is an “innovative way of combining diverse datasets in order to understand health and wellbeing” as set out in the Economic and Social Research Council’s long‐term strategic priorities (2009). 
The level of detail requested for this project (10-digit OACODE, split by age groups and gender) is more aggregated than the health data related census items (self‐rated health status, long‐term disability, provision  of unpaid care) that the Office for National Statistics (ONS) releases as open data without any registration.
HES data will be used in order to evaluate two key concepts: Health service use and evaluated health.  As for the first concept of 'health services use', for every group of patients in an output area, the number of inpatient and outpatient visits will be analysed in relation to their internet use.  As regards the second concept of 'evaluated health', a relative measure of the wellbeing of the population will be analysed based on the available admission and discharge diagnoses.  No individual analyses will be done, only aggregated output areas will be analysed.
Specific outputs expected, including target date(s): 
The outcomes of the research will be written up as a doctoral thesis (DPhil at the University of Oxford).  Results may be published or included in presentations, and the thesis will be deposited both in print and online in the University archives to facilitate its use in future research.  No record-level data will be disseminated, only aggregated results based on output area level.
Based on the research, a dataset will be produced that will be stored by the Oxford Internet Institute but will not be accessed by other researchers.  The dataset will contain information on individual, anonymised people's internet use and information on the respective output area based on the census data and HES data.
According to the requirements of the University of Oxford and the ESRC (one of the funding bodies of the doctoral research), research data and records must be preserved for a minimum of 3 years after publication.
However, based on the specific circumstances in relation to confidential HES data, the researcher can confirm that the dataset obtained from the HSCIC will be discarded at the end of the project (at the end of the term of agreement), and any variables in the created dataset coming from HES data will be excluded from the final dataset that is deposited with the University.
Expected measurable benefits to health and/or social care, including target date(s): 
Internet use is considered to improve health (e.g. through looking up information for self‐care, changes in interactions with health professionals, or social support received online), but supporting evidence is scant. Consequently, this research seeks to shed light on this relationship by analysing the evidence for Internet use affecting health service use and patients’ self‐rated health status in England. The findings may inform the UK Government digital inclusion strategy2, which specifically mentions health benefits as one of their aims, as well as the ongoing NHS commissioned project “Widening digital participation”, in which 100,000 individuals are trained to use the Internet with the prospect of individual health benefits.
As health services (especially the NHS) move towards a ‘digital by default’ approach to providing information and access to services (such as online booking and personal health records), it is imperative that practitioners and policymakers understand associations between digital access (internet use) and measures of health (including use of health services, and health status). It is possible that digital access could improve health, through better information and improving access and engagement, but there is a possibility that internet use could cause inappropriate use of health services or could lead individuals to avoid seeking help when they need it. This current proposal is therefore needed as one of the very first large scale studies to explore if health related Internet use is indeed related to levels of health service use (from HES data).
The issues of digital exclusion/inclusion and the relationships between health‐related Internet use and health care are highly topical and of current interest to practitioners and policymakers (especially as NHS England embraces a “digital by default” vision for future services). With this in mind, the researcher believes that a general medical journal with a high impact such as the BMJ will be interested in these findings and this will be a key target journal. If unsuccessful, the researcher will seek publication in the leading Social Science and Medicine journal. 
In addition to academic publications, the researcher will also feedback the results of this research to the NHS England project “Widening Digital Participation”. The Programme Director, Bob Gann, has expressed specific interest in the findings of the project and has confirmed that they will be helpful in informing NHS England strategy in this area (see attached email). Additionally, the researcher has been in contact with Helen Milner (Chief Executive) and Kate Mason (Project manager) of the Tinder Foundation, the organisation commissioned by NHS England to conduct the “Widening Digital Participation” project.  The researcher will ensure that the results of the research are also fed back into the NHS via this route.  To reach a wider audience, the researcher also intends to disseminate the results at medical/public health conferences such as the Society for Social Medicine annual scientific meeting, the Lancet Public Health Science conference and the British Sociology Association Medical Sociology conference.
